stances.claim: BBM remained a public officer (Governor of Ilocos Norte) on March 18, 1986, when his ITR was due -- the Provisional Constitution kept incumbent officials in office until proclamation or designation/qualification of a successor, and Castor Raval was sworn in only as 'acting governor.'
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-text + sworn-record argument to defeat the 'exile relief' defense

stances.claim: BBM did not present proof that he was 'forced' to be exiled with his father; absent such proof, the exile narrative cannot excuse the March 18, 1986 filing failure.

BBM's 'No' answer to COC Item No. 22 is false because the question asks whether the offense 'carries with it' the accessory penalty -- not whether a court 'imposed' it. The conviction's offense in fact carries perpetual disqualification.
stances.rhetorical_move: close textual reading of the COC question

stances.claim: BBM cannot claim ignorance of the consequences of his conviction -- he appealed it to the CA and SC, and as a former Vice Governor, Governor, Member of Congress, and Senator he is presumed (under the Civil Code maxim Ignorantia juris neminem excusat) to know the law.

Jalosjos v. Comelec (Oct. 9, 2012) authorizes COC cancellation even where the candidate's eligibility was earlier upheld and he has previously served (e.g., twice as mayor) -- so BBM's past electoral wins are no shield.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban turns to the petitioners' motion for partial reconsideration of the Comelec Second Division's refusal to cancel BBM's Certificate of Candidacy, presenting and largely endorsing the arguments of counsel Theodore O. Te. Item 11 of BBM's COC ('I am eligible') and Item 22 ('No' to having been found liable for an offense carrying perpetual disqualification) are, the petitioners say, false material representations. Te counters the Second Division by arguing that the CA need not have expressly imposed the perpetual-disqualification penalty because it is 'deemed written into the conviction' by operation of law; that BBM remained a public officer on March 18, 1986 (the 1985 ITR filing deadline) under the Provisional Constitution, since Castor Raval was sworn in only as 'acting governor' of Ilocos Norte; and that abandonment of office is itself a felony -- 'exceedingly ludicrous' to invoke on the offender's behalf. Te further argues that COC Item 22 asks only whether the offense 'carries with it' the accessory penalty (it does) and that BBM, having appealed his conviction to the CA and SC (later withdrawn) and served as Vice Governor, Governor, Member of Congress, and Senator, is presumed to know the consequences -- 'Ignorantia juris neminem excusat.' Jalosjos v. Comelec (Oct. 9, 2012) authorizes cancellation even when past eligibility had been upheld. Panganiban records his own conviction with the petitioners' core claims, while noting one point ('This is debatable') where reasonable minds may diverge -- leaving the doctrinal-strategic posture pointed sharply at the Comelec en banc and ultimately the Supreme Court.
